title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC: Science-Focused Server GPU to Arrive in 2028
gist: NVIDIA announced at SC26 Rubin HPC, a 2028 vector-heavy (>50K CUDA cores), NVLink 7 GPU marking its return to HPC after sitting out Blackwell; FP64 performance is the key unknown, and AMD (MI430X, 2027) and Intel (D-Series) will compete.

insights.claim: NVIDIA announced at SC26 a dedicated HPC-optimized GPU, Rubin HPC, based on the Rubin architecture and slated for release in 2028.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms NVIDIA intends to compete for 2028+ supercomputer procurements, which are typically decided years in advance.
insights.quote: the future chip will be an HPC optimized version of the company’s Rubin GPU architecture
insights.locator: Adding to a busy SC26 conference

insights.claim: Rubin HPC would be NVIDIA's first significant HPC-class GPU since the Hopper generation, roughly four years earlier; NVIDIA all but sat out the HPC market with Blackwell.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A multi-year gap in NVIDIA HPC product left room for rivals to win supercomputer contracts in the interim.
insights.quote: After the company all but sat out the HPC market with its Blackwell generation of parts
insights.locator: Consequently, NVIDIA’s announcement of a dedicated HPC chip

insights.claim: NVIDIA's Rubin HPC announcement signals it does not intend to permanently cede the HPC and supercomputer market to AMD and Intel, which have been splitting that market in recent years.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Expect renewed NVIDIA pricing/competitive pressure on AMD and Intel HPC wins from 2028.
insights.locator: Consequently, NVIDIA’s announcement of a dedicated HPC chip

insights.claim: Because commercial GPU server demand has shifted to AI and low-precision math over the last half-decade, server GPU designs have favored tensor cores, leaving traditional science and engineering users with fewer hardware options.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AI-driven chip design has under-served the HPC niche, creating an opening for HPC-specific products.
insights.quote: This has left traditional science and engineering users with fewer options than they have previously enjoyed

insights.claim: Rubin HPC will have more than 50,000 CUDA cores, roughly twice as many as NVIDIA's current flagship Rubin SoC and versus 18,944 on B200 and 16,896 on H200.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a vector-heavy die aimed at FP64/FP32 science workloads rather than AI tensor throughput.
insights.locator: The headline news here is that NVIDIA’s future HPC chip

insights.claim: Few HPC workloads can make heavy use of matrix multiplication and tensor cores, so an ideal HPC processor must be a strong vector processor, not just a tensor processor.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Use vector FP64 throughput, not AI TOPS, to judge competitiveness of HPC accelerators.
insights.quote: An ideal HPC processor needs to be a great vector processing machine and not (just) a tensor processing machine
insights.locator: The headline news here is that NVIDIA’s future HPC chip

insights.claim: NVIDIA's FP64 performance has plateaued at a bit under 40 TFLOPS since Hopper, with Blackwell Ultra especially poor at under 2 TFLOPS FP64; the key Rubin HPC metric to watch is FP64 vector and tensor performance.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: FP64 figures when disclosed will determine whether Rubin HPC can win back supercomputer share.
insights.quote: Blackwell Ultra being especially poor here at less than 2 TFLOPS
insights.locator: Still, the top line figure to watch here

insights.claim: Rubin HPC's FP64 gains will depend on how many FP64 units NVIDIA builds in and how much die area it takes away from tensor cores; the author's spec table speculates fewer tensor cores than prior parts.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Die-area trade-off between AI and FP64 is the key design tension; an HPC part may be less attractive for AI.
insights.locator: Still, the top line figure to watch here

insights.claim: NVIDIA says Rubin HPC will support precisions from NVFP4 to FP64, implying low-precision AI formats will not be heavily compromised on the HPC chip.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: The chip may serve mixed HPC/AI workloads, broadening its addressable market beyond classic FP64 users.
insights.locator: In lieu of specific performance figures

insights.claim: NVIDIA briefly touted a 'sparse data acceleration' capability to keep Rubin HPC's cores fed, apparently distinct from existing tensor-core sparse matrix support, without giving details.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: An undisclosed feature to watch for at future disclosures.

insights.claim: Rubin HPC will support NVLink 7, a generation beyond the NVLink 6 on NVIDIA's current Rubin server GPU, and NVIDIA is pitching a 'balanced design' scaling compute and data movement together.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Scale-up interconnect remains NVIDIA's differentiator versus AMD and Intel in HPC.

insights.claim: The author infers Rubin HPC is likely closer to a derivative of Rubin Ultra, the first chip to ship with NVLink 7, than of the original Rubin server chip.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Rubin Ultra disclosures may preview Rubin HPC capabilities.
insights.quote: the 2028 Rubin HPC chip following it will be closer to a Rubin Ultra derivative
insights.locator: Reading between the lines a bit

insights.claim: The 2028 timing would give Rubin HPC access to HBM4e memory rather than the HBM4 used on current Rubin, and NVIDIA's render suggests 8 HBM stacks across multiple dies.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Additional HBM4e demand from HPC parts in 2028 for memory suppliers.

insights.claim: NVIDIA will face HPC competition from AMD's HPC-focused Instinct MI430X launching in 2027 and Intel's PCIe-based GPU D-Series, giving rivals a head start before Rubin HPC's 2028 arrival.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: AMD's 2027 MI430X has a timing advantage in supercomputer procurements before NVIDIA's part ships.
insights.quote: they will have a fight on their hands if they want to retake a large portion of the HPC market
